subtopic: Drawn into a high-control group or online extremism
passage:
Gopika called Arnab at eleven at night from outside the group's hostel in Salt Lake. She had one bag. 'Can I come to you? Just for tonight.'
He was there in forty minutes in a borrowed car. He didn't ask why. He didn't say I told you so.
On the drive she talked in pieces. The promised job at the group's school had never come, after three years. She was so tired she'd fallen asleep standing in the prayer hall. And Arnab had kept sending her cricket scores every Sunday, no matter what.
The next weeks were practical. He cleared the spare room. He helped her write a CV that didn't have a three-year hole in it, and forwarded two openings from his office. When she couldn't decide what to eat without asking someone, he found a counsellor who worked with people leaving such groups and went with her to the first appointment.
He never once said the group's name with a sneer.

qa.q: How long did it take Arnab to arrive?
qa.a: He was there in forty minutes in a borrowed car.

qa.q: What does Gopika's trouble deciding what to eat suggest about her state?
qa.a: It suggests the group had taken over her choices for so long that she has lost confidence in her own judgement.

qa.q: Which kinds of support from Arnab made leaving possible and safe?
qa.a: No blame, patient listening, a room to stay in, help with her CV and job openings, and going with her to a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt, sending cricket scores every Sunday with no reply for years?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and sometimes hopeless, but kept going because he wanted her to know someone outside still cared.

grounding: It shows a young woman leaving after a broken promise and exhaustion, supported by a trusted friend with no blame, practical help and counselling.

passage:
'Nitin? It's past midnight. Where are you?'
'Bus stand. Near the flyover.' His voice cracked. 'I left, Hafsa. I just walked out.'
'Stay there. I'm coming.'
Twenty minutes later she found him on a bench, shoes untied, a plastic bag of clothes on his lap.
'I'm so tired,' he said. 'Five years. They said the new centre would be ours. It went to the leader's cousin.'
'You don't have to explain now.'
'You kept messaging. Even when I told you to stop.'
'I know.'
'Aren't you going to say you were right?'
'No.' She sat beside him. 'You can sleep at my aunt's place tonight. She has a spare room. Tomorrow we'll sort out your phone and ID.'
'I don't have a job. I don't know what I think about anything.'
'That's okay. There are counsellors who help with exactly this. We'll go together.'
Nitin leaned forward, head in his hands, and breathed.

qa.a: She found him on a bench at the bus stand, near the flyover.

qa.q: How does Nitin feel as he sits at the bus stand?
qa.a: He feels exhausted, betrayed by the broken promise about the centre, and lost about what he thinks.

qa.q: What made Hafsa's support helpful rather than harmful?
qa.a: She didn't blame or say she was right, listened, arranged a safe place to sleep and help with ID, and offered to go with him to a counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Hafsa to keep messaging Nitin when told to stop?
qa.a: It was probably painful and uncertain, but her steady contact made her the trusted person he called when he left.

grounding: It shows a young man leaving after a broken promise and exhaustion, supported by a trusted friend who offers no blame, practical help and counselling.
